title: Policy Engines
text:
Comparison with Synchronisation Tools
While policy engines operate directly on emerging digital objects, synchronisation tools serve a different purpose. Services such as OneDrive, Dropbox, Google Drive, or Nextcloud‑based platforms like SURFdrive replicate files across devices for convenience, but they do not manage:

metadata

identifiers

provenance

lineage

policy‑driven placement

multi‑site coordination

Sync tools solve convenience and collaboration problems.
Policy engines solve digital‑object lifecycle problems.

title: Policy Engines
text:
Summary
Storage systems keep files safe, but they cannot manage metadata, replicas, identifiers, or the volatile stages where research data is created and transformed. To manage data as digital objects, two complementary systems are needed.
Data repositories (Dataverse, Figshare, Invenio/Zenodo) curate and publish stabilised datasets. They provide structured workflows, metadata templates, DOIs, and governance, but they operate mainly at the dataset level and are not designed for active, changing data.
Policy engines (iRODS, Rucio, Globus, Starfish) coordinate files, metadata, and storage during active research. They support replication, tiering, ingest rules, lineage tracking, and metadata‑driven automation across distributed systems. They treat files as emerging digital objects long before publication, ensuring that key lifecycle events are governed and recorded.
Unlike synchronisation tools, which simply replicate files for convenience, policy engines manage the full digital‑object lifecycle.






TipPolicy engines in a nutshell



A policy engine governs active research data by coordinating files, metadata, and storage. It applies rules for replication, placement, retention, and lineage, and forms digital objects either at ingest (storage‑centric) or after discovery (observation‑centric). Rather than handling every file operation, it governs the key lifecycle events that make data trackable, reproducible, and consistently managed across systems.


Even with repositories and policy engines enriching and exposing metadata to some extent, metadata still becomes fragmented across institutions and disciplines. Each repository, workflow platform, policy engine manages metadata locally. Without additional infrastructure, this creates isolated pockets of metadata that cannot be searched or linked across systems.
To avoid these silos, research ecosystems rely on metadata services that collect, normalise, and aggregate metadata from many sources. These services enable cross‑repository discovery and make metadata visible beyond the system where it was created.
How they achieve that, we will doscover in the next chapter.

title: Metadata Infrastructure
text:
Portals, Harvesters, Indexers, and Serialisation
Metadata becomes truly powerful only when it can be shared, discovered, aggregated, and reused across systems. For this to work, research infrastructures rely on a set of services that collect, expose, and standardise metadata at scale. These services form the metadata infrastructure that underpins FAIR data ecosystems.
This chapter introduces the main components of that infrastructure: metadata portals, metadata harvesters, indexing services, and the serialisation formats that allow metadata to move between systems.

title: Metadata Infrastructure
section: Why Local Metadata Alone Is Not Enough
text:
Why Local Metadata Alone Is Not Enough
Creating a metadata record inside a repository is essential, but metadata that stays inside a single system remains effectively invisible to the wider research ecosystem. A dataset may be perfectly documented, but if its metadata is not exposed in standardised, machine‑readable ways, it cannot be:

discovered by search engines

harvested by aggregators

indexed by disciplinary or cross‑disciplinary portals

linked to related datasets, publications, or software

integrated into knowledge graphs

found by researchers outside the hosting institution

In other words, metadata is only as useful as the infrastructure that distributes it.
Several factors limit the findability of “local‑only” metadata:

Siloing — each repository stores metadata in its own database, often with its own schema

Lack of standardisation — metadata may not follow common schemas or vocabularies

No machine‑readable exposure — metadata may be visible on a webpage but not accessible via APIs or harvesting protocols

No cross‑repository search — users must know the repository exists before they can find the data

No integration with PID services — identifiers may not be resolvable or linked to global discovery systems

This is why FAIR emphasises that metadata must be findable and accessible, not merely present.
To achieve this, repositories must expose metadata through standard protocols (e.g., OAI‑PMH, ResourceSync, REST APIs) so that external services can collect and index it.

title: Metadata Infrastructure
text:
Metadata Portals
Metadata portals are platforms that provide human‑ and machine‑readable access to metadata records. They act as central entry points for discovering datasets, publications, software, and other research outputs.
Portals typically:

expose metadata through search interfaces

provide landing pages for datasets

offer APIs for programmatic access

integrate controlled vocabularies and ontologies

link metadata to identifiers such as DOIs, ORCID iDs, and ROR IDs (see Chapter Persistent Identifiers)


Examples

DataCite Commons — aggregates metadata for DOIs assigned to datasets, software, and publications

OpenAIRE Explore — integrates metadata from repositories across Europe

FAIRsharing — registry of metadata standards, databases, and policies

Discipline‑specific portals (e.g., PANGAEA, GBIF, ICPSR)

Portals are the public face of metadata: they make research outputs discoverable and provide the context needed for reuse.

title: Metadata Infrastructure
text:
Metadata Harvesters
Metadata harvesters solve the visibility problem by collecting metadata from many repositories and bringing it together into a unified index. They ensure that metadata created locally becomes part of a broader, interoperable ecosystem.
Harvesters typically:

poll repositories at regular intervals

retrieve metadata records using standard protocols

normalise or enrich metadata

detect updates, deletions, and new versions

feed metadata into search indexes or knowledge graphs


Common harvesting protocols

OAI‑PMH (Open Archives Initiative Protocol for Metadata Harvesting)
Widely used in repositories; supports incremental harvesting and multiple metadata formats.
ResourceSync
A modern protocol for synchronising large collections of metadata and content.
REST APIs
Many repositories expose metadata through JSON‑based APIs.



Examples of harvesters

OpenAIRE Harvester — collects metadata from thousands of repositories

DataCite OAI‑PMH service — exposes DOI metadata for harvesting

Europeana Harvester — aggregates cultural heritage metadata

Harvesters are the connective tissue of metadata infrastructure: they ensure that metadata does not remain siloed.

title: Metadata Infrastructure
text:
What Is a Metadata Indexer?
A metadata indexer is a service that takes harvested metadata and organises it into a searchable, structured index.
Indexers:

parse metadata into fields

normalise identifiers (e.g., DOI, ORCID, ROR)

enrich metadata with external information

build search indexes (e.g., Elasticsearch, Solr)

support faceted search, filtering, and ranking

may generate knowledge graphs or entity‑resolution layers

In short:
Harvesters collect metadata; indexers make it findable.

Examples

OpenAIRE Graph — a large‑scale scholarly knowledge graph integrating publications, datasets, software, and projects

DataCite Search Index — supports DOI discovery and metadata enrichment

Google Dataset Search — indexes structured metadata exposed on the web

Semantic indexes built on RDF triple stores (e.g., Blazegraph, GraphDB)

Indexers turn metadata into actionable information, enabling discovery, analytics, and automated linking.

title: Metadata Infrastructure
text:
Metadata Serialisation Formats
To move metadata between systems, it must be expressed in serialisation formats that machines can read. These formats encode metadata according to schemas, ontologies, and controlled vocabularies.
Serialisation formats fall into two broad categories:

1. Key–Value and Document‑Oriented Formats
These formats are widely used in repositories, APIs, and metadata templates.

JSON — common for REST APIs; flexible and human‑readable

XML — used in OAI‑PMH, DataCite XML, Dublin Core XML

YAML — popular in research workflows and documentation

CSV / TSV — often used for simple metadata templates or variable‑level metadata

These formats are easy to generate and consume, but relationships between entities are implicit.


2. Semantic Web and Linked Data Formats
These formats express metadata as graphs, enabling interoperability and machine reasoning.

RDF/XML

Turtle (TTL)

JSON‑LD

N‑Triples / N‑Quads

These formats encode metadata as subject–predicate–object triples, using URIs to identify entities. They are used in:

knowledge graphs

ontology‑driven metadata

schema.org markup for dataset discovery

provenance tracking (e.g., PROV‑O)



Why serialisation matters
Serialisation determines:

how metadata is exchanged between systems

how easily it can be validated

whether it supports Linked Data

how well it integrates with harvesters and indexers

In practice, repositories often support multiple serialisations to serve different use cases.
Below we give an example of the same metadata expressed in different formats.


Example: The Same Metadata in JSON, XML, and Turtle
Below we describe a fictive dataset using three common serialisation formats.
The metadata fields are:

license: CC BY 4.0

- No explicit semantics

</resource>
Characteristics:
- Hierarchical structure
- Often validated with schemas (e.g., XSD)
- Still no explicit semantics unless combined with namespaces


Turtle (RDF / Linked Data)

@prefix ex:     <http://example.org/> .

- Suitable for knowledge graphs and FAIR Linked Data

When to Choose Which Serialisation Format?
Different serialisation formats serve different purposes, and the right choice depends on how the metadata will be used.
JSON is ideal when metadata needs to be exchanged quickly and flexibly between systems. It is the natural choice for REST APIs, lightweight services, and modern repositories because it is easy to generate, easy to parse, and widely supported by programming languages.
XML is preferred when metadata must follow a strict schema and be validated against a formal structure. Many harvesting protocols (such as OAI‑PMH) and long‑standing metadata standards (like Dublin Core XML or DataCite XML) rely on XML because of its predictability and strong validation capabilities.
YAML works well for human‑authored metadata, such as workflow descriptions, lab templates, or configuration files. It is readable and concise, but less suitable for large‑scale automated processing.
CSV/TSV is the simplest option for tabular or variable‑level metadata. It is easy to create and edit, especially for researchers working in spreadsheets, but it cannot express hierarchical or semantic relationships.
RDF serialisations such as Turtle, JSON‑LD, and RDF/XML are the best choice when metadata needs to be interoperable, machine‑interpretable, and semantically rich. They allow metadata to be integrated into knowledge graphs, linked to ontologies, and connected across systems using globally unique identifiers. JSON‑LD is particularly useful for embedding semantic metadata on the web, while Turtle is preferred for human‑readable Linked Data.
In practice, many repositories support multiple serialisations: a simple JSON or XML representation for APIs and harvesting, and a semantic RDF representation for Linked Data and FAIR interoperability. The choice depends on whether the priority is ease of use, strict validation, or semantic richness.

title: Metadata Infrastructure
section: A Note on Linked Data, Triple Stores, and Combining Knowledge Graphs
text:
A Note on Linked Data, Triple Stores, and Combining Knowledge Graphs
Linked Data changes how metadata is shared and connected across research infrastructures. Instead of exchanging whole records through harvesting protocols, repositories can publish their metadata directly as RDF using persistent identifiers (DOIs, ORCID iDs, ROR IDs) and shared vocabularies. This allows metadata to be expressed as a graph, where entities are nodes and their relationships are edges.
Repositories can expose RDF in several ways:

Static RDF files (e.g., Turtle or JSON‑LD generated on demand or published as dumps)

Content negotiation (e.g., returning RDF when a client requests text/turtle or application/ld+json)

API endpoints that output RDF serialisations

SPARQL or Linked Data endpoints when the repository uses a graph‑based backend

Only the last option requires a triple store; the others simply generate RDF from the repository’s internal metadata model.
A triple store is a specialised database designed to store and query RDF triples—statements in the form subject–predicate–object. It supports SPARQL queries, reasoning, and graph traversal, and can automatically merge graphs from different sources when they use the same identifiers. If two repositories describe the same dataset, person, or organisation using the same URI, a triple store treats them as the same node. No custom mapping or harmonisation layer is required; the semantics are embedded directly in the data model.
This makes combining knowledge graphs remarkably straightforward. Multiple RDF sources can be loaded into the same triple store, and shared identifiers cause the graphs to interlink automatically. The infrastructure does not need to normalise formats, deduplicate records, or align schemas—the graph model handles this naturally.
Because of this, Linked Data reduces the need for traditional metadata harvesters. A harvester normally collects XML or JSON from many repositories, normalises it, deduplicates it, and prepares it for indexing. In a Linked Data environment, much of this work disappears: repositories publish RDF, and the triple store ingests it directly. The infrastructure no longer needs to “fix” metadata during harvesting.
However, this convenience for infrastructures shifts responsibility upstream. For Linked Data to work well, researchers and data stewards must provide clean identifiers, consistent vocabularies, and well‑structured RDF. Instead of the infrastructure harmonising metadata after the fact, the quality and interoperability of the combined graph depend on the metadata producers themselves.
In short: triple stores make integration easier for infrastructures, but require more discipline and modelling effort from researchers. When done well, the result is a metadata ecosystem that is inherently connected, machine‑interpretable, and ready for reuse across systems.

title: Persistent Identifier Services
text:
When to Assign a Persistent Identifier
Persistent Identifier (PID) services are a fundamental component of modern research infrastructures and Research Data Management (RDM) systems. They provide stable, globally unique identifiers for digital and organizational entities within the research ecosystem. These entities include datasets, publications, software, researchers, institutions, research projects, and funding information.
A persistent identifier ensures that a digital object can be reliably referenced, discovered, and accessed over time, even if its physical location changes. PID services are typically operated by international organizations and integrated into repositories, publishing platforms, and research infrastructure services. By assigning persistent identifiers to digital objects and actors, these systems enable reliable citation, linking between resources, and automated machine processing.
Persistent identifiers also play a central role in enabling interoperable and FAIR‑compliant research infrastructures.
In this chapter we will focus on PIDs and PID services for digital objects, i.e. data. A general overview over PIDs can be found in the chapter Persistent Identifiers.
When implementing an RDM service or infrastructure component, persistent identifiers directly support the FAIR Data Principles, particularly the first principle:
F1. (Meta)data are assigned a globally unique and persistent identifier. “Principle F1 is arguably the most important because it will be hard to achieve other aspects of FAIR without globally unique and persistent identifiers.”
However, not every piece of data produced during research requires a PID immediately. During early stages of the research data lifecycle, datasets may still be experimental, incomplete, or subject to frequent changes. Assigning persistent identifiers too early can lead to unnecessary versioning and administrative overhead.
A PID should typically be assigned once data becomes a stable digital object. Common situations in which a persistent identifier should be assigned include:
At this stage the digital object becomes part of the scholarly record and benefits from stable identification, discoverability, and citation.

Persistent Identifier Systems and Services in the Research Ecosystem
Multiple persistent identifier (PID) systems exist to uniquely identify entities within the research ecosystem. Some focus on research outputs such as datasets and publications, while others identify people, institutions, or research activities. Below we list several PID systems commonly used for referencing datasets and digital objects.

DOI (Digital Object Identifier)
The Digital Object Identifier (DOI) system, managed by the DOI Foundation, is one of the most widely used PID schemes in scholarly communication.
DOIs are primarily used to identify digital research outputs, including:

datasets

journal articles

software

reports

The DOI system is built on top of the Handle System, which provides the underlying resolution infrastructure.
Two major DOI registration agencies are widely used in research data management:

DataCite – primarily assigns DOIs to datasets and research data

Crossref – primarily assigns DOIs to scholarly publications

Example DOI:
10.5281/zenodo.3238330


EPIC (European Persistent Identifier Consortium)
The European Persistent Identifier Consortium (EPIC) provides PID services based on the Handle System infrastructure. EPIC is widely used in European research infrastructures and data services.
EPIC identifiers are typically used for:

identifying digital objects in research infrastructures

supporting long-term access to research data

linking datasets and research resources across distributed infrastructures

Common users include:

European research infrastructures

research data repositories

e-science services

Example EPIC Handle:
21.T11998/0000-001A-3905-F


Handle System
The Handle System is a technical resolution infrastructure developed by the Corporation for National Research Initiatives (CNRI). It provides the distributed, persistent lookup mechanism used by several PID schemes.
The Handle System underpins:

the DOI system

the EPIC PID service

It is widely used by:

repositories

digital libraries

research infrastructures



ARK (Archival Resource Key)
The Archival Resource Key (ARK) is a separate PID system, distinct from the Handle System. It was developed by the California Digital Library and is widely adopted in libraries, archives, and cultural heritage institutions.
ARKs are commonly used for identifying:

digital collections

archival objects

digitized cultural heritage materials

Unlike DOIs and EPIC identifiers, ARKs do not rely on the Handle System. They use their own resolution approach, typically through ARK-enabled service providers.
Example ARK:
ark:/12345/x54

Spotlight on Handles, EPICs, DOIs
Persistent identifier (PID) infrastructures for digital resources are built on layered technical and governance frameworks. Systems such as the Digital Object Identifier (DOI), the Handle System, and services provided by EPIC operate within the broader conceptual framework of the Digital Object Network Architecture (DONA). Together they form an ecosystem that enables stable identification, management, and resolution of digital objects on the internet.

Figure 14.1: The main organisations DONA, EPIC and DOI





The Handle System provides the underlying technical infrastructure for persistent identifiers. It enables globally unique identifiers, known as handles, to be assigned to digital objects and resolved through a distributed network of handle servers. When a handle is queried, the system returns associated metadata, such as the current URL of the resource. This separation between the identifier and the object’s location ensures persistence even when the resource moves.
Built on top of the Handle System is the Digital Object Identifier (DOI) system, a widely used persistent identifier scheme for scholarly publications, datasets, and other research outputs. DOIs use the handle protocol for resolution but add additional governance, metadata standards, and registration workflows tailored to scholarly communication. Organizations such as International DOI Foundation oversee the DOI framework and coordinate registration agencies that assign DOIs to digital objects.
The European Persistent Identifier Consortium (EPIC) is another major provider of persistent identifiers based on the Handle System. EPIC operates a handle registration service primarily aimed at research institutions, data infrastructures, and e-science projects in Europe. Unlike the DOI system, which focuses heavily on scholarly publishing workflows, EPIC provides a more general handle-based PID service that can be used for datasets, research infrastructures, software, and other digital assets.
At the architectural level, both DOI and EPIC-based handles operate within the principles of the Digital Object Network Architecture (DONA). DONA defines a global infrastructure for digital object management, including the assignment of identifier prefixes, governance of the handle registry, and operation of root resolution services. Through DONA, different identifier communities—such as DOI registration agencies and EPIC handle services—can coexist while sharing the same global resolution infrastructure.
In summary, DONA provides the overarching framework for managing digital object identifiers. The Handle System supplies the technical resolution mechanism within this framework. DOI represents a specialized, widely adopted identifier scheme built on handles, while EPIC operates as a consortium that provides handle-based persistent identifier services, particularly for European research infrastructures. This layered ecosystem enables long-term, interoperable identification and access to digital resources across diverse domains.

title: Persistent Identifier Services
section: Different Use of the Handle System: EPIC vs DOI
text:
Different Use of the Handle System: EPIC vs DOI
Although both European Persistent Identifier Consortium (EPIC) and the Digital Object Identifier (DOI) system use the Handle System for identifier resolution, they use the Handle record in different ways.

EPIC: Metadata in the Handle Record
EPIC uses the Handle System as a full PID infrastructure, meaning that the Handle record itself stores meaningful metadata about the object. EPIC follows the PID Information Types model, which standardizes how information is encoded in Handle records.
Example Handle:
21.T11998/0000-001A-3905-F
A Handle record in EPIC may include multiple typed entries such as:








Type
Example Content
Purpose




URL
https://repository.org/object/123
Current location of the object


CHECKSUM
sha256:...
Data integrity verification


EMAIL
contact@repository.org
Administrative contact


10320/LOC
Multiple URLs
Location-aware resolution


PID_INFO_TYPES
Reference schema
Declares metadata structure



In this model, the Handle record itself functions as a lightweight metadata container, enabling machines to retrieve essential information directly from the Handle infrastructure.


DOI: Metadata Outside the Handle Record
In contrast, the DOI system uses the Handle System primarily for resolution, not for storing descriptive metadata.
A DOI such as:
10.1000/182
is technically implemented as a Handle, but the Handle record typically contains only minimal information, most importantly:



Type
Content




URL
Landing page of the resource



The actual metadata for the DOI (title, authors, publication date, publisher, etc.) is stored in external metadata registries managed by DOI Registration Agencies such as Crossref or DataCite.
These agencies maintain large metadata databases that can be queried through APIs. For example:

Crossref metadata API
DataCite metadata store

When someone resolves a DOI through doi.org, the Handle system simply redirects the user to a landing page, while the rich metadata is retrieved from the registration agency’s infrastructure rather than from the Handle record itself.
The difference can be understood as two architectural approaches:








Feature
EPIC Handles
DOIs




Infrastructure
Handle System
Handle System


Metadata location
Inside the Handle record
External metadata registries


Metadata model
PID Information Types
DOI metadata schemas


Resolution
Directly from Handle record
Redirect to landing page


Example prefix
21.*
10.*



Thus, EPIC uses the Handle System as a metadata‑aware PID infrastructure, designed to support interoperability across research infrastructures and to maintain actionable links between data objects, services, and workflows. In contrast, the DOI system uses the Handle System primarily as a resolution layer, while the descriptive metadata and publication‑oriented services are maintained in separate, domain‑specific registries such as DataCite and Crossref.
Whereas DOIs are embedded in the scholarly publishing ecosystem—complete with citation metadata, indexing in bibliographic databases, and integration with publication workflows—EPIC identifiers are optimized for technical interoperability, enabling research infrastructures to reference, connect, and manage data objects across distributed systems. In other words, DOI focuses on publication, discoverability, and metadata indexing, while EPIC focuses on infrastructure‑level persistence, machine‑actionable metadata, and cross‑system integration.

We can see how the Handle System is used differently in practice by comparing two PIDs: 10.5281/zenodo.3238330 and 11304/3185a834-5178-41bf-a849-b9ddbe4c5638.
The first identifier is a DOI. If we resolve it through the Handle System using https://hdl.handle.net/10.5281/zenodo.3238330?noredirect we can inspect the metadata stored directly in the Handle record.



Example DOI


This record contains two standard fields:

HS_ADMIN — an administrative entry that defines

which Handle identity (usually the prefix administrator) controls the handle
what permissions that identity has
which operations they are allowed to perform. This entry is part of every Handle record, whether it belongs to EPIC, DOI, or another service.

URL — the target location the resolver redirects to when the handle is used.

Every Handle record includes at least these two entries.
Now let’s look at 11304/3185a834-5178-41bf-a849-b9ddbe4c5638 - an EPIC example:



Example EPIC


Here we again see the mandatory HS_ADMIN and URL fields. In addition, the organisation responsible for this prefix has added extra information. These additional fields come from a custom PID profile used by EUDAT for their B2SHARE data publishing service.
In this case, the PID points directly to a file and includes useful details such as the file’s checksum. This allows users or systems to verify the file’s integrity, for example during data migration or when downloading the file.

title: Persistent Identifier Services
text:
Resolution of Persistent Identifiers
To understand how persistent identifiers function behind the scenes, it helps to look at how a resolver retrieves the information stored in a Handle record. Resolution is simply the process of turning an identifier into the current location or metadata of the object it represents.
Using the Handle System as an example, the process works like this:
When a user enters a Handle such as 21.T11998/0000-001A-3905-F into a resolver—or clicks a link containing it—the request is sent to the global Handle infrastructure operated by the Corporation for National Research Initiatives (CNRI).






%%{init: {
  "look": "handDrawn",
  "flowchart": { "htmlLabels": false }
}}%%

flowchart TB

    REQ[Browser: Send request<br>10.5281/zenodo.3238330]
    PREFIX[Lookup prefix 10.5281 at global Handle server]
    LOCAL[Contact local server<br>which hosts all PIDs for 10.5281]
    RECORD[Get handle record]
    REDIR[Redirect to resource in URL field]

    REQ --> PREFIX --> LOCAL --> RECORD --> REDIR





Figure 14.3: The Handle resolution





The resolver then performs a series of steps:

Request submission
The user or application sends the Handle to a resolver service.
Prefix lookup  The resolver checks the prefix (the part before the slash) to determine which Handle server is responsible for that identifier.
Local server query  The resolver contacts the appropriate server and requests the Handle record.
Record retrieval
The server returns the stored entries—typically including a URL pointing to the current location of the object, along with administrative fields such as HS_ADMIN.
Redirection
Using the URL entry, the resolver redirects the user or system to the resource’s current location.

Because the Handle record can be updated whenever the underlying resource moves, the identifier itself remains stable. This is the same principle described in the previous chapter: the PID stays the same, only the target information changes, ensuring long‑term access even as systems evolve.
Understanding resolution tells us how a PID behaves once it exists. The next step is to look at how such identifiers come into being. This brings us to the two core building blocks of the Handle System: minting a Handle and managing the Handle record.

title: Persistent Identifier Services
text:
Minting Handles
Minting a Handle means creating and registering a new persistent identifier for a digital object.
Organisations participating in the Handle System receive a prefix (for example from EPIC). They then generate a unique suffix for each object they want to identify. Together, these form a globally unique Handle:
prefix/suffix

Prefix – identifies the organisation responsible for the identifier

Suffix – uniquely identifies the object within that organisation

Example:
21.T11998/0000-001A-3905-F
Once minted, the Handle is registered in the global Handle infrastructure and can be resolved using the mechanism described in the previous chapter.

title: Persistent Identifier Services
text:
The Handle Record
Every Handle points to a Handle record, which stores the information needed for resolution. At minimum, a record contains:

a URL entry, indicating where the resolver should redirect the user

an HS_ADMIN entry, defining who controls the Handle and what permissions they have

Depending on the use case, additional entries may be included.
For example, EPIC Handles often store:

checksums

protocol information

service endpoints

machine‑actionable metadata

This flexibility allows Handles to describe not only web resources but also files, collections, workflows, or non‑HTTP services.
When the location of a digital object changes, only the Handle record needs to be updated.
The identifier itself remains stable, ensuring persistent and reliable access over time. The same is actually also true for all other information which is captured in the PID metadata.

section: Practical Example: Creating an EPIC Handle and Managing Its Metadata
text:
Practical Example: Creating an EPIC Handle and Managing Its Metadata
To demonstrate how Handle‑based PIDs are created and managed in practice, this example uses pyhandle, a Python library developed by EUDAT.
EUDAT maintains large‑scale European research data services, and pyhandle is their official client library for interacting with EPIC Handle services through the Handle REST API.
Before you can mint Handles, you need credentials issued by your Handle service provider (for example, EPIC or a local institutional Handle server). These credentials typically include:

the Handle prefix assigned to your organisation

a username associated with that prefix

a private key or password for authentication

optional permissions for reverse lookup or administrative actions

They are usually delivered as a small JSON file (often named credentials.json) that pyhandle can read directly.
With that context in place, the following steps show how to mint a Handle, add metadata, update its target location, and manage non‑HTTP resources.

1. Install the Python Library
!pip install pyhandle



2. Imports
from pyhandle.clientcredentials import PIDClientCredentials
from pyhandle.handleclient import PyHandleClient



3. Connect to the Handle Server
Here we load the credential file provided by EPIC (or your institutional Handle service) and create a client authenticated for minting and updating Handles.
cred = PIDClientCredentials.load_from_JSON("credentials.json")
client = PyHandleClient('rest').instantiate_with_credentials(cred)



4. Minting a Handle
handle = client.generate_PID_name(cred.get_prefix())
print(handle)
Example output:
21.T12996/a70da9ee-1202-451f-89ba-37d907fea470



5. Adding Metadata
meta = {"checksum": "blablabla"}
meta["URL"] = "http://google.com"
client.register_handle_kv(handle, **meta, overwrite=False)



6. Updating Handle Metadata
yoda_data_loc = "https://data.yoda.uu.nl/research-christine/my_books/"
meta["data_type"] = "collection"
meta["protocol"] = "webdav"
meta["URL"] = yoda_data_loc
client.modify_or_add_handle_value(handle, **meta)
Delete metadata:
client.delete_handle_value(handle, "checksum")



7. Minting EPIC Handles for Non‑HTTP Resources
EPIC allows Handles to describe resources that are not directly accessible via HTTP, such as iRODS paths or WebDAV collections. In such cases, the Handle may include protocol‑specific metadata and a URL that points to a resolver landing page rather than the resource itself.
handle2 = client.generate_PID_name(cred.get_prefix())
meta2 = {
    "protocol": "iRODS",
    "irods_path": "/uu/home/research-christine/my_books",
    "irods_server": "data.yoda.uu.nl",
    "URL": f"https://hdl.handle.net/{handle2}?noredirect"
}
client.register_handle_kv(handle2, **meta2, overwrite=False)
Example:
21.T12996/24c4010d-1527-409b-953b-8c8548d3330a



8. Searching and Managing Handles
Some Handle services allow reverse lookup, meaning you can search for Handles based on metadata values (e.g., a URL or checksum). This requires additional credentials with search permissions.
search_client = PyHandleClient("rest").instantiate_for_read_and_search(
    handle_server_url="https://your.local.handle.server",
    reverselookup_password="your_password",
    reverselookup_username="21.T12996"
)
result = search_client.search_handle(URL="/myfile/here/local.txt")
print(result)

title: RDM Platform
text:
What FAIR Means for Infrastructure
From Components to a FAIR‑Aligned Infrastructure
Modern Research Data Management (RDM) is built from many specialised components: repositories, policy engines, metadata services, PID services, and storage systems. Each plays a distinct role, but none of them delivers FAIR on its own. FAIR only emerges when these components are assembled into a coherent platform with shared standards, predictable data flows, and consistent governance.
When these systems interoperate through stable APIs, shared schemas, and coordinated policies, they stop being isolated tools and become a platform: an environment where data can move, evolve, and be reused without losing identity, metadata, or provenance.
This is the shift from components to infrastructure design.
Designing a modern RDM platform means taking the FAIR principles seriously—not as guidelines for researchers, but as requirements on the infrastructure itself. A FAIR‑aligned platform is therefore not a single system but a coordinated ecosystem that makes data Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable by design.
FAIR is often interpreted as a metadata‑centric framework, but for infrastructure, FAIR applies equally to files, formats, and the protocols and workflows that produce them. A digital object is not only metadata + PID; it is also:
A FAIR‑aligned infrastructure must therefore support metadata FAIRness, file FAIRness, and protocol FAIRness simultaneously.

title: RDM Platform
text:
the files themselves

the formats they use

the methods and processes that generated them

the relationships that bind these elements together



Findable (F1–F4)
To make data findable, infrastructure must support persistent identifiers (F1) such as DOIs or Handles, ensuring that datasets remain citable and identifiable even as they move across storage systems. These identifiers must be accompanied by rich metadata (F2) that describes the dataset in a structured, machine‑readable way. Metadata must explicitly link back to the dataset it describes (F3), and both data and metadata must be registered in searchable indexes (F4) that can be harvested by external services.
Findability also applies to files.
Infrastructure must ensure that:

files have stable internal identifiers

file‑level metadata (format, size, checksums) is indexed

formats are recognisable and documented

files remain findable within datasets and workflows

This ensures that users and machines can locate not only the dataset, but also the specific files and components it contains.


Accessible (A1–A2)
Accessibility requires that data and metadata be retrievable through open, standardised protocols (A1), such as HTTPS, S3, WebDAV, or OAI‑PMH. These protocols must be free to implement (A1.1) and support authentication and authorisation where needed (A1.2). Even if data becomes restricted or removed, its metadata must remain accessible (A2), ensuring that the scholarly record is preserved.
Authentication and Authorisation Infrastructure (AAI) plays a central role here. AAI ensures that users whether humans or machines can access data in a controlled, auditable way. It provides:

authentication (confirming who the user is)
authorisation (determining what they may access)
federation (allowing users to log in with institutional or community identities)

AAI is therefore a core part of FAIR Accessibility, enabling secure access without compromising openness. Inthe chapter Authentication and Authorisation Infrastructure we provide an introduction.
For files, accessibility means:

files must be retrievable via stable URLs or API endpoints

formats must be open or well‑documented so they can be accessed in the future

versioning must ensure that older file versions remain accessible

checksums and fixity information must be available to verify integrity

For protocols and workflows, accessibility means:

descriptions of methods, instruments, and computational steps must be accessible

workflow definitions and parameters must be retrievable

provenance must be accessible so results can be reproduced

This ensures that data can be accessed and understood long after its creation.


Interoperable (I1–I3)
Interoperability is achieved when infrastructure supports formal, shared languages (I1) such as RDF, JSON‑LD, or XML, enabling machines to understand and combine metadata from different sources. Metadata must rely on FAIR vocabularies and ontologies (I2), which include:

generic vocabularies such as Dublin Core or schema.org

domain ontologies from communities such as the OBO Foundry, a collaborative initiative that develops interoperable, well‑structured ontologies for biology and related fields

These vocabularies provide stable identifiers and shared semantics, allowing metadata to be interpreted consistently across systems. Interoperability also requires qualified references (I3) that link datasets to related entities such as software, instruments, or grants.
For files, interoperability requires:

use of open, community‑accepted formats

format validation and conversion workflows

machine‑readable descriptions of file structure (e.g., ISA‑Tab, DDI, JSON‑LD)

For protocols and workflows, interoperability requires:

structured descriptions of experimental or computational steps

standard ways of expressing inputs, outputs, and parameters

machine‑readable provenance linking files to the processes that generated them

Together, these elements require APIs, ontology support, and metadata models capable of expressing rich, typed relationships between files, workflows, samples, and datasets, not just flat metadata fields.


Reusable (R1–R1.3)
Reuse depends on rich descriptions (R1) that capture domain‑specific details using community standards such as ISA or DDI. Metadata must include a clear usage license (R1.1), detailed provenance (R1.2), and conform to community expectations (R1.3).
For files, reuse requires:

formats that can be opened and interpreted in the future

clear versioning and fixity information

technical metadata (MIME type, encoding, resolution, units)

links to the workflows or instruments that produced them

For protocols and workflows, reuse requires:

complete descriptions of experimental or computational methods

software versions, parameters, and environment details

links between inputs, outputs, and intermediate steps

machine‑actionable provenance

Infrastructure must therefore support schema versioning, provenance capture, workflow integration, and controlled vocabularies for licensing not only for metadata, but also for files and protocols.

title: RDM Platform
section: Integration and Policy: The Glue That Makes FAIR Work
text:
Integration and Policy: The Glue That Makes FAIR Work
A FAIR data platform is only FAIR if its components work together. This requires well‑defined integrations and an orchestration layer that governs how data and metadata move across the lifecycle. Storage, metadata services, policy engines, and repositories must interoperate through stable interfaces and shared standards so that data remains coherent as it transitions between systems.
APIs alone are not enough.
APIs allow systems to exchange data, but they do not guarantee that:

identifiers remain stable across components

provenance is captured at the moment data moves

metadata stays bound to files

lifecycle events are recorded consistently

transformations and transfers are traceable

When components communicate only through ad‑hoc API calls, the digital object effectively “falls apart” at each system boundary. Provenance becomes fragmented, identifiers drift, and metadata must be reconstructed or is lost entirely. The platform may appear integrated, yet behaves like isolated tools stitched together by point‑to‑point connections.
A FAIR‑aligned infrastructure therefore needs:

Clear integration contracts (APIs, event streams, metadata mappings, PID handling)

Consistent metadata models across all layers

Automated workflows for validation, provenance, versioning, and access control

An orchestration layer to coordinate:

ingest from active storage

metadata enrichment

transformations and quality checks

publication to repositories

synchronisation across catalogs and indexes


With this orchestration layer, the platform becomes a coherent, predictable, auditable, FAIR‑by‑design ecosystem.
Without it, digital objects lose their identity and provenance in the gaps between services.

title: RDM Platform
section: Transitions in the RDM Lifecycle: Where FAIR Is Won or Lost
text:
Transitions in the RDM Lifecycle: Where FAIR Is Won or Lost
The importance of orchestration becomes clear when looking at the transitions that occur throughout the research data lifecycle. These lifecycle transitions, e.g moving from active data to archived data, from FAIRified metadata to a published dataset, or from a repository to a discovery portal, almost always correspond to transitions between components of the RDM platform.
Each transition is a point where the digital object is most vulnerable.
Every time data crosses a system boundary, the platform must preserve:

the identity of the object

the metadata that describes it

the provenance that explains how it was produced

If any of these fail, FAIRness breaks down.
Two challenges dominate these lifecycle transitions:

1. Preserving the identity of the digital object
Not every system in the research workflow needs to treat files as fully formed digital objects.
During early, active phases such as work in synchronisation services or collaborative file shares researchers often work with working copies, drafts, and temporary outputs. In these environments, strict digital‑object identity is not required; files may change rapidly, and identifiers may not yet be assigned.
However, once a digital object is formed, its identity must remain stable and traceable as it moves through the RDM lifecycle. From that point onward, every service must recognise the object as the same entity. This requires:

early or timely PID assignment when the object stabilises

stable internal identifiers for files and collections

consistent PID handling across systems

mappings that prevent re‑minting or duplication

If identifiers diverge after the digital object is formed, the object fractures into multiple incompatible versions across storage, workflows, repositories, and portals. This breaks traceability, provenance, and ultimately FAIRness.
In short:
working copies may be fluid, but digital objects must be stable.
Once identity is established, it must persist across all transitions.


2. Ensuring metadata travels with the object
Many systems like storage, workflow engines and transfer tools are file‑centric. They move bytes, not digital objects. Without orchestration:

metadata becomes detached

provenance is lost

FAIRification must be repeated

discovery and reuse collapse

A FAIR‑aligned platform must therefore ensure that:

metadata is bound to the object through identifiers

metadata is carried forward at each transition

file‑centric systems can still reference metadata via PIDs

metadata is enriched, not overwritten

provenance is captured automatically

This requires shared metadata models, identifier schemes, and exchange formats across all components.


Why transitions and orchestration belong together
Lifecycle transitions and component transitions are two views of the same events.
The orchestration layer ensures that these transitions are:

governed

recorded

consistent

lossless

Without orchestration, the digital object loses coherence as it moves across the platform.
With orchestration, it remains identifiable, described, linked, and traceable from creation to publication and beyond.

title: Digital Object Continuity
text:
Where the Digital‑Object Layer Breaks Without Orchestration
Even when individual components are well designed, an RDM platform that relies only on APIs, i.e. without a shared digital-object layer and orchestration, cannot guarantee that identity, metadata, and provenance remain intact across transitions. The following examples illustrate how and where the digital object breaks when systems exchange data but do not share lifecycle state.

title: Digital Object Continuity
text:
Failure Modes in API‑Only Transitions

1. Policy Engine → Repository: Duplicate Publications and Lost Lifecycle State
A policy engine manages active data and often forms digital objects early in the lifecycle. A repository manages publication, curation, and long‑term preservation. When the two are connected only through an API, neither system has visibility into the other’s lifecycle state.
This leads to several failure modes:

the same dataset can be published multiple times

the repository may mint multiple DOIs for the same object

the policy engine cannot see whether a dataset is still a draft, under review, or already published

provenance becomes fragmented: the repository sees a “new upload”, not a continuation of the same object

The root cause is simple:
the policy engine and the repository do not share a digital‑object identity or a shared lifecycle model.
The repository treats each API upload as a new object, creating a new identifier for the same data; the policy engine assumes it is handing over the same one, while not being able to establish that with the repository.
Result:
The digital object forks into multiple versions, each with its own identifiers and metadata.


2. Synchronisation / Sharing Service → Repository or Policy Engine: Working Copies Drift Away From the Digital Object
Synchronisation and file‑sharing services are designed for working copies, not for maintaining the authoritative representation of a digital object. They allow:

renaming

moving

deleting

overwriting

restoring older versions

resolving sync conflicts

sometimes even metadata tagging

All of these are legitimate user actions in a sync environment.
The problem is not that the digital object in the policy engine or repository becomes unstable, it remains stable, but that its connection to the original working files becomes unreliable if the sync service is treated as a source of truth.
When a repository or policy engine ingests files from a sync service via an API:

files may disappear from the sync service after ingestion

files may be renamed, breaking the mapping between working copies and the ingested object

files may be overwritten, so the working copy no longer corresponds to the preserved version

folder structures may change, breaking assumptions about context or metadata extraction

sync conflicts may create duplicate or partial files, making it unclear which version was ingested

In this scenario:

the digital object in the repository or policy engine is stable,

but the working copies in the sync service are not.

This means the digital object loses its connection to the evolving working environment, and the sync service cannot be relied upon to reflect the authoritative bitstreams.
It is therefore essential that once a digital object is formed, the repository or policy engine becomes the single source of truth for the bitstreams.
The sync service may continue to hold working copies, but it must not be treated as the authoritative representation.
Result:
The digital object remains stable, but its link to the working copies breaks as the sync service cannot guarantee persistence, identity, or provenance for the files it holds.


3. Repository / Policy Engine → Metadata Service: Two Sources of Truth for Metadata

Metadata services aggregate metadata from repositories, policy engines, and other systems.
If they only expose metadata, the digital‑object layer remains intact:

But if the metadata service is also used to enrich, modify, or extend metadata, the digital object now has two competing sources of truth:

the repository/policy engine holds one version

the metadata service holds another

This creates several failure modes:

metadata becomes out of sync

updates in one system are not propagated to the other

identifiers may be linked inconsistently

provenance may be split across systems

portals may expose stale or conflicting metadata

Once two systems can modify metadata independently, the digital object no longer has a single, authoritative description.
Result:
The digital object’s metadata diverges, and FAIRness collapses at the semantic level.

text:
Why These Failures Occur
All three examples share the same underlying issue:

APIs move data, but they do not preserve digital‑object identity, metadata binding, or provenance across systems.

Without orchestration:

each component sees only its local view

no system knows the full lifecycle state

identifiers drift

metadata forks

provenance becomes incomplete

the digital object loses coherence

This is why a FAIR‑aligned platform must treat the digital object as a shared, governed entity, not an emergent side effect of API calls.

title: Digital Object Continuity
section: Ensuring Continuity Across the Lifecycle Through an Orchestration Layer
text:
Ensuring Continuity Across the Lifecycle Through an Orchestration Layer
The failure modes described in the previous sections duplicate DOIs, unstable working copies, metadata divergence, and fragmented provenance are not isolated accidents. They are symptoms of a deeper architectural problem: most current RDM infrastructures treat digital objects as local constructs, defined independently by each service. APIs move files and metadata, but they do not preserve identity, metadata binding, provenance, or lifecycle state across system boundaries.
This is the current state of the art in many research environments:
systems exchange data, but they do not share a digital‑object model.
As a result, digital objects fracture as they move.
The international FAIR Digital Object (FDO) community has been working to solve exactly this problem. Their work—formalised in the FDO‑IP (FAIR Digital Object Interoperability Principles)—provides a conceptual and technical foundation for ensuring that digital objects remain coherent across the entire lifecycle, regardless of how many systems they pass through.
An orchestration layer is the architectural mechanism that implements these principles in practice.

title: Digital Object Continuity
section: The Problem: RDM Systems Without a Shared Digital‑Object Layer
text:
The Problem: RDM Systems Without a Shared Digital‑Object Layer
In today’s typical RDM ecosystem:

repositories mint new identifiers for objects they receive

policy engines cannot see lifecycle state downstream

metadata services enrich metadata without propagating updates

sync services mutate working copies unpredictably

provenance is trapped in local logs

lifecycle state is implicit, inconsistent, or missing

Each system sees only its own local view.
No system knows the full lifecycle.
No system is responsible for continuity.
This is precisely the fragmentation that the FDO community set out to address.

title: Digital Object Continuity
section: The FDO Vision: Digital Objects as Governed, Machine‑Actionable Entities
text:
The FDO Vision: Digital Objects as Governed, Machine‑Actionable Entities
The FAIR Digital Object model proposes a simple but transformative idea:

A digital object should be a governed entity with a persistent identity, typed metadata, lifecycle state, and provenance independent of the system currently holding its files.

An FDO is defined by:

a persistent, globally unique identifier

a typed, machine‑actionable object record

bound metadata that travels with the object

explicit lifecycle state

cross‑system provenance

standard interfaces for accessing and updating the object

The FDO‑IP formalises these requirements into a set of interoperability principles that any system can adopt.
The orchestration layer is the architectural component that enforces these principles across an RDM platform.

title: Digital Object Continuity
text:
FAIRDOM‑SEEK in the RDM Architecture
The failure modes above show how easily digital objects fragment when transitions rely only on APIs and when each system maintains its own local view of identity, metadata, and lifecycle state.
In response to these challenges, some research communities, especially the life sciences, have taken a different architectural path. Instead of distributing responsibility for identity, metadata, and provenance across multiple loosely connected systems, they developed platforms that minimise transitions during active research.
The FAIRDOM‑SEEK community exemplifies this strategy.

Rather than moving digital objects between many services, SEEK provides a single environment where identity, metadata, context, and provenance are created and maintained together throughout active research.

By reducing the number of handovers, SEEK reduces the opportunities for identity drift, metadata forking, and provenance loss.
This approach does not eliminate transitions entirely, but it postpones them until the digital object is mature, when the risks are lower and the need for continuous provenance is less critical.
FAIRDOM‑SEEK therefore occupies a hybrid space in the RDM ecosystem.
It was built by and for the life sciences community, where research objects are complex and interdependent: samples, assays, protocols, models, workflows, and multi‑step experimental designs all need to be linked and contextualised long before formal publication.
Because of this complexity, SEEK does not fit neatly into a single RDM category.
Instead, it combines capabilities traditionally associated with:

repositories (stable identifiers, landing pages, versioning)

policy engines (structured organisation, access control, workflow‑aware provenance)

metadata services (semantic annotation, ISA structures, machine‑actionable metadata)

Its purpose is not to replace these components, but to bridge the gap between active research and publication, ensuring that digital objects become richly contextualised and machine‑actionable before they enter preservation‑oriented systems.

FAIRDOM‑SEEK and FAIR Data Station operate in the FAIRification and digital‑object layer, where research outputs are enriched, contextualised, and prepared for publication. They provide internal discovery but do not perform long‑term archiving or cross‑platform metadata aggregation. When preservation or large‑scale aggregation is required, SEEK relies on standard external services such as institutional or domain repositories, archiving platforms, and metadata portals.

How SEEK Combines Aspects of Multiple RDM Components

Repository‑like capabilities

optional DOI minting

versioning and static URLs

structured landing pages

metadata exposure via Bioschemas, schema.org, RDF



Policy‑engine‑like capabilities

structured organisation of files and research assets

project‑level access control

workflow‑aware provenance (via RO‑Crate)

integration with workflow engines



Metadata‑service‑like capabilities

creation, validation, and enrichment of metadata

semantic annotation and ontology‑backed fields

ISA‑based structuring of investigations, studies, and assays

machine‑actionable metadata export (JSON‑LD, RDF, RO‑Crate)

Because they combine these capabilities, SEEK operates in the FAIRification and contextualisation layer — the transitional space where raw files become structured, semantically rich research objects.
This is the same space where, in the examples above, digital objects break when transitions rely only on APIs. SEEK helps prevent such failures by binding identity, metadata, and context early in the lifecycle.



RO‑Crate vs. OAIS‑Style Archival Packaging
A key reason SEEK sits between categories is their use of RO‑Crate, a packaging format optimised for FAIR metadata, semantic relationships, and research‑object context.
Repositories and archives, by contrast, rely on OAIS‑aligned standards such as METS, PREMIS, and BagIt, which focus on long‑term preservation and fixity.

SEEK therefore sits naturally between active research systems and repositories.


Publishing in SEEK vs. Publishing in a Repository
Because SEEK operates in the FAIRification layer, “publishing” in these systems serves a different purpose than publishing in a repository.


Publishing in FAIRDOM‑SEEK (RO‑Crate‑centric)

Focus on context, ISA structure, samples, models, protocols

Assets interlinked into a research graph

Metadata exposed via Bioschemas, RDF, SPARQL, JSON API

Optional DOI minting

Not designed for long‑term preservation

SEEK publishes metadata‑rich research objects, not archival datasets.


Publishing in a Repository (OAIS‑aligned)

Focus on dataset‑level publication

DOI mandatory

Long‑term preservation guaranteed

Metadata harvested by global portals

Curation workflows ensure quality

Archival packaging (BagIt, AIP) ensures fixity

Repositories publish archival digital objects that enter the scholarly record.


Why This Hybrid Role Matters for Transitions
By combining features from repositories, policy engines, and metadata services and by being purpose‑built for the life sciences SEEK:

support FAIRification early in the lifecycle

provide semantic depth that repositories typically do not create

stabilise metadata before publication

prepare research objects for preservation and discovery

reduce the burden on repositories by delivering structured, validated metadata

integrate smoothly with workflow engines and policy engines

reflect the complexity and interconnectedness of life‑science research objects

They do not replace repositories or policy engines; they complement them by ensuring that digital objects are contextualised, semantically rich, and machine‑actionable before they enter the publication and preservation layers.

title: Digital Object Continuity
section: Architectural Principles for Robust RDM Transitions
text:
Architectural Principles for Robust RDM Transitions
A FAIR‑aligned RDM platform succeeds or fails in the transitions between components.
This chapter showed that when systems exchange data only through APIs—without a shared digital‑object layer, i.e. identity, metadata, and provenance can fragment across boundaries. The solution is not to build more isolated services, but to design platforms that treat transitions as first‑class architectural concerns.
Three principles follow from this.

1. Good platform design matters
RDM infrastructure is not simply a collection of tools.
It is an ecosystem in which digital objects must remain identifiable, contextualised, and traceable as they move across services.
Designing for this continuity requires:

stable identifiers

metadata binding

lifecycle‑aware orchestration

predictable, governed transitions

clear contracts for how services interact

A platform that preserves these elements across transitions behaves as a coherent whole, even if its components are heterogeneous.


2. Plan Transitions Carefully to Avoid Creating New Silos
Before introducing a new service, the key architectural question is not:

“What features does this tool provide?”

but rather:

“How does this service interface with the rest of the platform or eco system, and how does it participate in the lifecycle of a digital object?”

A service that cannot preserve identity, metadata, and provenance across boundaries risks becoming another silo—even if it is excellent at what it does internally.
Designing for transitions means:

understanding upstream and downstream dependencies

ensuring identifiers and metadata remain stable

avoiding duplication of lifecycle state

preventing multiple sources of truth

This mindset shifts the focus from tool‑centric design to ecosystem‑centric design.


3. Discipline‑specific platforms are valuable, but must expose standards
Systems like FAIRDOM‑SEEK and FAIR Data Station show how discipline‑specific platforms can provide deep, domain‑appropriate FAIRification.
Their strength lies in supporting the complexity of life‑science research objects: samples, assays, workflows, models, and protocols.
But they remain interoperable because they expose:

standard identifiers (DOIs, ORCID, internal stable IDs)

standard metadata models (ISA, JSON‑LD, schema.org, Bioschemas)

standard packaging (RO‑Crate)

standard APIs

standard provenance structures

This ensures that domain‑specific platforms can be combined with repositories, policy engines, and metadata portals from other disciplines without losing coherence.
In other words:

Discipline‑specific does not mean discipline‑isolated.
A platform can be tailored to a community while still participating in a broader, interoperable RDM ecosystem.



4. Always ask: How does this platform or service interface with others?
Every component in an RDM platform should make its interfaces explicit:

What identifiers does it accept and emit?

How does it expose metadata?

How does it receive lifecycle state, and how does it pass it on?

Does it enrich metadata, or only expose it?

Does it act as a source of truth for files, metadata, or provenance?

How does it ensure that downstream systems can maintain continuity?

A service that answers these questions clearly can be integrated into a FAIR‑aligned ecosystem.
A service that cannot risks breaking the digital‑object layer.


In short

Design is important: digital objects must remain coherent across transitions.

Think transitions before building a new silo: tools must integrate into the lifecycle, not sit beside it.

Discipline‑specific platforms are valuable: but only if they expose standards that allow them to interoperate with services from other domains.

Interfaces matter: every service must make clear how it participates in the lifecycle of a digital object.

This sets the stage for the next chapter, where we look at metadata portals and aggregation services, and how they depend on well‑designed transitions to provide global discovery.
